stories.headline: Trump Questions Integrity of Midterm Elections Days After Saying He Would Accept Results
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump questioned the legitimacy of the midterm results on Monday, days after telling the New York Times on election night that he was "absolutely willing" to accept the outcome. "Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong?" he wrote on Truth Social. His post made vague references to polling, voting "dumps" and "machines" without citing specific evidence of error or wrongdoing.

Democrats retook both chambers of Congress in last week's elections. As it stands, they have won 54 Senate seats and 254 House seats, with counting continuing in some races, including Senate contests in Alaska and Mississippi. State and local officials across the country have said voting was mostly problem-free.

Election experts said the reporting of results followed normal patterns. MIT political scientist Charles Stewart III said the nation saw the standard patterns in when votes are reported. Ruth Greenwood of Harvard's Election Law Clinic said slower counts in some states do not mean anything nefarious is occurring.

Trump has said he would have won easily had he been on the ballot, and has acknowledged on Fox News that the Iran war contributed to Republican losses, saying voters were unwilling to accept paying more for gasoline. Trump has long argued that voter fraud is rampant, while studies and election officials say it is extremely rare. Democrats and many election officials have rejected his claims, while Trump's supporters have often said concerns about election procedures deserve scrutiny.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Keeps US 'Locked and Loaded' on Iran as Rubio Defends Hegseth
stories.summary:
The Trump administration is maintaining military pressure on Iran through a naval blockade and the deployment of a new aircraft carrier, even as the president has said renewed escalation is unlikely if talks make progress. Fox News reported that Trump described the United States as "locked and loaded" while diplomacy continues.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking to reporters in Paris on Monday, defended War Secretary Pete Hegseth amid calls from some lawmakers for his impeachment. Rubio said Hegseth "works really hard" and "is incredibly smart," and pointed to the Pentagon's role in counter-cartel efforts in the Western Hemisphere.

Rubio also cited damage to Iran's military as evidence of Hegseth's performance. "They have no navy, they have no air force," he said, adding that Iran still retains some capabilities but is "very degraded" compared with a year ago. He acknowledged that people can have different views politically.

The developments follow weeks of limited US strikes on Iranian air defenses, enforcement of the blockade in the Gulf of Oman, and a behind-the-scenes push led by Vice President JD Vance for a ceasefire and nuclear talks. Critics of the Iran campaign point to higher gasoline prices and political costs, while supporters argue that military pressure is necessary to force concessions from Tehran.

stories.headline: Russia's Leading Independent Newspaper Novaya Gazeta Closes After Eviction
stories.summary:
Novaya Gazeta, Russia's leading independent newspaper, has closed after being evicted from its offices and facing sustained pressure from authorities. On Monday, its staff held a final editorial meeting before packing up their belongings and leaving.

For 30 years the paper published investigations into corruption, human rights violations and abuse of power. Its co-founder, Nobel Peace Prize winner Dmitry Muratov, spoke to the BBC about the closure.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov responded by saying Russia's media landscape is highly diverse and that the closure was part of "a standard rotational process." Press freedom advocates and critics of the government have long described the pressure on independent outlets in Russia as a campaign to silence dissent.

The closure removes one of the last major independent domestic voices in the country's media, at a time when Russia remains at war in Ukraine and peace talks are under way in Abu Dhabi.

stories.headline: US Stocks Rally, Recovering Most of Last Week's Losses as Oil Prices Fall
stories.summary:
U.S. stocks rallied Monday, with the S&P 500 jumping 2.3% for a second straight gain. The advance recovered most of last week's steep losses, which stemmed from worries that Democratic victories in the midterm elections could slow the construction of AI data centers.

Oil prices swung lower during the session, helping support the market. Axios analysis of FactSet data noted that the long-running link between daily oil price moves and Treasury yields has broken down in recent weeks.

Axios said the shift suggests growth risks may be supplanting inflation worries as the dominant economic concern. Investors are weighing how a Democratic Congress could affect technology spending, regulation and the broader economy.

Separately, Axios reported that Elon Musk's business empire faces political risks from Democratic oversight following the midterms.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Lifts Block on Big Bend Border Wall Construction, Weighs Limits on Suing Federal Officials
stories.summary:
The Supreme Court on Monday handed the Trump administration a win on its emergency docket by lifting a lower court order that had paused border wall construction in the Big Bend region of southwest Texas, including areas in and around Big Bend National Park. U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone, an appointee of President George W. Bush, had blocked three waivers issued by the Department of Homeland Security while the underlying case proceeded. The justices halted her decision from last month in a brief statement, allowing construction to continue.

The order does not end the litigation. Environmental groups that sued to stop the project say the barrier threatens a remote and ecologically sensitive landscape, and their lawsuit continues in the lower courts. The administration has argued that it needs to proceed with a signature border security project, and supporters of the wall have framed the ruling as a validation of the executive branch's authority to waive environmental requirements. Critics and conservation advocates have objected to building in a national park.

Separately on Monday, the court heard oral arguments in a case brought by a former Hawaii inmate seeking damages from a prison nurse who allegedly ignored his medical needs. The justices appeared unlikely to allow the claim to go forward, but some signaled reluctance to abandon entirely the decades-old Bivens precedent, which allows federal officials to be held individually liable for violating constitutional rights. A ruling is expected by the end of the term and could shape whether inmates and others can sue federal employees for constitutional violations.

stories.headline: Update: White House Cautiously Optimistic as Russia-Ukraine Talks Resume in Abu Dhabi
stories.summary:
U.S. officials said Monday the White House is "cautiously optimistic" as peace talks between Russia and Ukraine resume in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday. The sessions will be the first time the parties have met with U.S. mediators present since February, when negotiations were suspended because of the war in Iran. White House envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have worked for weeks to persuade Russian President Vladimir Putin to return to the table.

According to a senior U.S. official, Russian and Ukrainian envoys will discuss territorial issues and proposals for monitoring a ceasefire. The talks follow a localized truce last month around the Russian-occupied southern city of Oleshky, which allowed some trapped residents to be evacuated and humanitarian supplies to be delivered. President Trump said in a "60 Minutes" interview that the two sides are "very close" to a deal.

The diplomacy comes as Russian missile and drone strikes have continued to hit Ukraine's power grid and rescue workers ahead of the meetings. Territorial questions have been the central obstacle in earlier rounds, and it remains unclear whether either side will accept concessions. Officials have offered no timeline for an agreement.

stories.headline: Steel Factory Explosion Near Izmir, Turkey, Kills at Least 17
stories.summary:
At least 17 people were killed and 12 others injured in an explosion at the Habas Demir Celik iron and steel plant in Aliaga, near the western Turkish port city of Izmir. All of the dead and injured were workers at the facility, one of Turkey's leading steel producers. Footage showed a large fire inside the plant and a tall column of smoke.

Izmir Governor Suleyman Elban said the blast occurred around midday after a crane carrying a replacement boiler collapsed, causing materials to fall into a furnace below. The company said the accident happened during scheduled maintenance on one of the plant's electric arc furnaces. Some people were believed to remain under rubble, and search and rescue operations continued.

President Recep Tayyip Erdogan first put the death toll at 16 after a cabinet meeting, and Health Minister Kemal Memisoglu later said a critically injured worker had died, raising it to 17. Turkish media reported at least five arrests as investigations got under way. Workplace accidents are a chronic problem in Turkey, according to the independent Turkish Health and Safety Labor Watch.

stories.headline: Update: Republicans Face Difficult Lame-Duck Session After Midterm Losses
stories.summary:
Republicans return to Washington this week facing what Axios describes as an especially weak lame-duck session after a bruising midterm election that started a countdown on their control of Congress. Democrats have little incentive to help Republicans advance their agenda before January, when the new Congress is seated.

Departing GOP lawmakers could complicate matters further by skipping votes or defying party leaders. As a result, most items on the to-do list, including a looming shutdown deadline, could be pushed to the new Congress. Leadership fights inside the House and Senate Republican conferences add to the uncertainty.

Democrats, meanwhile, are positioning for the new session and have signaled plans for sustained oversight of the administration. Some commentators on the right argue the party needs to rethink its direction ahead of 2028, while Republican leaders say they intend to pursue priorities where possible. Funding for the government remains the most pressing deadline.

stories.headline: Two arrested after vehicle crashes onto sidewalk near White House
stories.summary:
A vehicle crashed onto a sidewalk near the White House on Monday morning, prompting a response from the Secret Service and National Guard and the closure of roads around the presidential residence. Responders arrived just before 10 a.m. at the north side of Lafayette Park, near 16th and H Streets NW, according to a Secret Service spokesperson.

The driver was combative with law enforcement but was quickly arrested. A second individual jumped a barricade near the northwest corner of Lafayette Park around the same time and was also taken into custody. The Metropolitan Police Department's Explosive Ordnance Disposal team swept the vehicle as a precaution, and roads surrounding Lafayette Park were closed.

White House journalists were ordered inside the building around 10 a.m. while the security response unfolded. Details remain unclear, including what prompted the crash, why the driver was in the area, and whether either person posed a specific threat to the White House. The Secret Service said both incidents remain under investigation, and further details are expected as officials complete their inquiries.

stories.headline: France accuses Iran's Revolutionary Guard of supermarket refrigeration cyberattack
stories.summary:
France has accused Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of being behind cyberattacks that raised temperatures in supermarket fridges and freezers. Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot called the attack "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression" and said those responsible would face sanctions at the European level. France summoned the Iranian ambassador to lodge a "very strong protest." Iran has not yet responded.

On 11 October, hackers took control of software regulating refrigeration units, hitting more than 100 Cooperative U stores and 180 Intermarche and Netto stores, with Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc also affected. The targeted software was supplied by Danish firm Danfoss, and in some stores temperatures reportedly reached 50C overnight, spoiling food worth millions of euros. A second wave earlier this month hit more than 100 stores in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland, though it is not known whether the incidents are linked.

Separately, the Paris prosecutor, Laure Beccuau, said an investigation has been opened into the head of an offensive cyber unit tied to the IRGC, named as Shahid Kaveh, and his two deputies. Barrot called it the first large-scale sabotage cyberattack on French territory and promised proportionate measures to deter repeats. Reuters has reported that fridge malfunctions at a small number of US military bases in August are also being investigated as possible deliberate attacks.

stories.headline: Update: Hegseth to hold press conference as Massie pushes impeachment; Senate GOP leadership vote in dispute
stories.summary:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced he will hold a Pentagon press conference Tuesday morning to address efforts to impeach him. Asked whether he has enough Republican support to defeat impeachment, he said, "We're not worried about that," and urged reporters to come "loaded for bear." Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., a critic of the Iran war and of Hegseth's performance, is expected to push impeachment efforts this week.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Sunday he is a "hard yes" on impeachment, arguing Hegseth "abused his power" and "engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran." Hegseth and the administration have defended the military campaign against Iran.

Elsewhere, Attorney General Todd Blanche said the Justice Department will not "stop working with Congress" under the incoming Democratic majority, responding to questions about oversight. In the Senate, Republicans led by Ron Johnson, with Mike Lee, Ted Budd, John Kennedy and Rick Scott, asked Conference Chair Tom Cotton to delay leadership elections scheduled for 9 a.m. Tuesday in favor of a discussion of how candidates intend to lead, warning that proceeding otherwise would be "political malpractice."

stories.headline: Four killed in Gaza as sand embankment collapses onto displaced families' tents
stories.summary:
Three children and one woman were killed when a sand embankment collapsed onto tents at a displacement camp south of Deir al-Balah in central Gaza on Sunday night, the Hamas-run health ministry said. Five injured people were reportedly rescued. The Civil Defence initially reported five dead, including two women, before the ministry revised the toll Monday to one woman, identified as Tahrir Nabhan, and three children.

The collapse followed torrential rain on Saturday that reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents across Gaza. Civil Defence said water levels reached 1.5 meters in places and that responders could handle only 10% of 2,100 distress calls. It urged international organizations to provide safe shelter and move tents away from sandy slopes.

Rescuer Mustafa al-Masri said volunteers dug victims out with their bare hands. The International Organization for Migration's Karl Baker said Gaza's 2.1 million people are confined to about 30% of the territory, many living in areas that would be unsuitable under normal conditions. The incident comes amid funding shortages that have forced the World Food Programme to cut Gaza aid.

stories.headline: Trump Says Deportation Policy 'Might Have Been Too Tough' and Offers Immigration Deal to Democrats
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump said in a "60 Minutes" interview with CBS correspondent Ross Douthat, broadcast Sunday, that his deportation policies "might be too tough" and may have contributed to Republican losses in the midterm elections. Asked whether immigration cost his party, he answered, "I think it both helped and hurt." He said he wanted to work out a deal with congressional Democrats that could offer legal status to "good" immigrants, particularly those with good jobs, while standing by efforts to seal the border and target violent offenders.

The remarks sit uneasily with his elevation of Stephen Miller, the architect of the mass deportation campaign, to White House chief of staff, a job Miller starts Monday. Democrats, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, said they did not expect deportations to slow under Miller. Some Republicans, such as Rep. Marlin Stutzman of Indiana, have criticized Miller's tone and record. Trump also told the program he considered the Iran war a "good decision" in the long term and said hatred between Zelensky and Putin is a main obstacle to ending the Ukraine war.

The interview came as Congress returned from the election recess. Republicans face leadership elections after losing both chambers, a Dec. 11 government shutdown deadline, and a possible House vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which Jeffries said he strongly supports. Attorney General Todd Blanche declined to rule out prosecuting Democratic lawmakers who investigate administration officials, after Trump called their requests "extortion" and ordered a Justice Department probe. Democrats say they are exercising constitutional oversight, while Trump allies describe the investigations as partisan retaliation. Vance has blamed the losses on the Iran war and costs, a view Trump said did not affect their relationship.

stories.headline: Update: Nvidia Board Investigates CEO Jensen Huang Over Affair With Suspected Chinese Spy
stories.summary:
Nvidia's board has opened an independent investigation into CEO Jensen Huang after he admitted to a romantic relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believe was gathering information for Beijing. In a draft email to employees obtained by Axios, Huang wrote, "I was unfaithful to my wife," and apologized to his family and staff. The New York Times reported that U.S. officials concluded the woman, Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman, was a spy.

The board said it had no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. Its inquiry will examine whether Huang misled the board or shareholders about the relationship and whether concealing it affected the company's value, raising investor concern about his future. Nvidia, valued at roughly $4.5 trillion, shares fell more than 4 percent, and some investors said the matter could cloud the broader AI trade.

President Trump defended Huang on Sunday, calling him a "fine person" who has "done an amazing job for our country," though he said he had not discussed the allegations with him. Multiple members of Congress have called for investigations, and a closed-door congressional briefing was planned. A Chinese spokesperson rejected the spying claims at a Monday briefing. Questions remain over whether Huang will join Trump on an Asia trip next week.

stories.headline: Update: Pope Leo Delivers Veiled Rebuke of Milei's Austerity in Buenos Aires
stories.summary:
Pope Leo XIV, arriving in Buenos Aires on the second stop of a 12-day Latin American tour, said Argentina's economy "must be at the service of the people, rather than people being at the service of the economy." The remarks were a diplomatic but pointed critique of President Javier Milei's austerity program, which the Catholic Church has said hits the poorest hardest.

Leo urged particular concern for those affected by illness, dependency and disability, a veiled reference to cuts in disability assistance. He also said strengthening democracy requires a "willingness to listen" and "careful use of words," which appeared to rebuke Milei's combative style. Leaders, he said, must acknowledge the limits of the power entrusted to them.

Milei defended his libertarian policies, calling rights to life, liberty and property the backbone of Argentina's constitution, and said his government is avoiding "punishing the Argentines of tomorrow in order to benefit the Argentines of today." He struck a conciliatory tone toward the late Pope Francis, whom he once called "evil on earth," now describing him as "undoubtedly the most important Argentine in history." The visit comes three weeks after Leo had surgery for lung cancer; the Vatican says his doctors report the cancer has not spread. A first Mass in Buenos Aires is expected to draw more than a million people.

stories.headline: Russell Brand Sentenced to 10 and a Half Years for Rape and Sexual Assaults
stories.summary:
A London judge sentenced Russell Brand on Monday to 10 and a half years in prison for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others. The former comedian and actor was convicted last week on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, in a case brought by six women. The rape occurred in 2009.

The judge said Brand showed a "casual, arrogant disregard" for women's wishes. Brand rose to fame as a celebrity in the early 2000s and later became an anti-establishment commentator known for conspiracy-minded content.

The sentencing concludes a high-profile trial that drew wide international coverage and marks a dramatic fall for a figure once prominent in British television and Hollywood.

stories.headline: Update: Krakow Shooting Suspect Dies in Hospital
stories.summary:
The 24-year-old gunman suspected of killing six people in Krakow's Main Market Square has died in hospital, Polish police said. He died early Monday morning of injuries sustained when armed officers engaged him in a gunfight on Saturday. Officials said he was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning, which prevented a further massacre.

The six people killed were four women and two men. Four were Polish, and a British national and an Austrian woman were also among the dead. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said three more bodies were found at the suspect's home, later identified by police as his 53-year-old father, 52-year-old mother and 21-year-old sister. The suspect has not been officially named.

A Polish minister said early investigations indicated he was inspired by "far-right ideologies" and described him as an "ultra-nationalist." Polish media reported that he held a firearms permit and may have obtained the weapons from his family home. Sixteen people, including five foreigners, two police officers and the attacker, were taken to hospital, with the foreigners coming from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia.

Both injured police officers have reportedly emerged from comas. One of two surgeons who were eating nearby and rushed to help said his colleague saved the life of a gravely injured officer by stemming the bleeding by hand until an ambulance arrived. The suspect's death means he will not face trial, and investigators are expected to continue examining his motives and how he obtained the weapons.

stories.headline: ANC Records Worst-Ever Result in South Africa Local Elections
stories.summary:
South Africa's African National Congress recorded its worst showing in local elections since the end of apartheid, winning about 31% of the national vote. That is down from 46% in 2021 and far below the 65% it won two decades ago. ANC secretary-general Fikile Mbalula called the outcome "catastrophic," citing the high cost of living and saying the middle class had turned on the party in large numbers.

The ANC won a majority in just one of nine provinces, Limpopo, compared with six in 2021, and topped the vote in only two of eight cities, down from six. The Democratic Alliance came second with 25% and kept control of Cape Town. Former president Jacob Zuma's MK party took 10% and unseated the ANC as the leading party in Durban, while Julius Malema's Economic Freedom Fighters finished fourth with 6%. Turnout was 52%, up from 46% in 2021.

President Cyril Ramaphosa said he accepted "the will of the people" with humility and called the decline concerning. The ANC lost its parliamentary majority in 2024 and now governs in a coalition Government of National Unity. Analyst Susan Booysen said the result sends a "devastating message," attributing the slide largely to poor service delivery, including failures in water, power and sanitation.

The results raise questions about the stability of the coalition and the ANC's prospects ahead of the next national contest, while the Democratic Alliance's overall vote share rose only marginally.

stories.headline: At Least 34 Dead After Europe-Bound Migrant Boat Sinks Off Senegal
stories.summary:
At least 34 people died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of Senegal, the Senegalese Press Agency reported, citing an official source. The interior ministry said one person was rescued and that the number still missing had not been established. The small wooden boat capsized between Dakar and the northern city of Saint-Louis while heading for Spain's Canary Islands.

Saliou Diouf, founder of the migrant aid group Boza Fii, told AFP that all bodies recovered so far were Senegalese, and search operations continue. President Bassirou Diomaye Faye expressed condolences, urged citizens not to risk the crossings, and pledged to intensify efforts to dismantle the smuggling networks, while also creating reasons for young people to hope at home.

The sinking comes as the Atlantic route remains the deadliest monitored by the Spanish group Walking Borders, which recorded 635 deaths between January and May 2026. On Saturday, a state of emergency was declared on Spain's El Hierro island after more than 3,300 people arrived in about 30 boats since the start of November, almost a third of the island's population. Canary Islands president Fernando Clavijo called the situation "absolutely unsustainable."

Senegalese authorities also intercepted another boat on Friday carrying 142 migrants. Tighter controls and cooperation between European and North African states may have diverted more journeys onto the Atlantic route.

stories.headline: Japan and Vietnam Agree to Deepen Economic Security and Energy Ties
stories.summary:
Japan and Vietnam agreed to deepen cooperation in trade, technology, defense and energy security as their leaders met in Tokyo on Monday. Vietnam's To Lam was visiting the Japanese capital for the talks.

The two governments said they aim to strengthen economic and strategic ties amid rising regional geopolitical and trade tensions. The agreement spans several areas that both countries consider central to economic resilience, including supply chains, technology and energy.

Further details of the agreements were not immediately available. The meeting reflects broader efforts by Asian economies to diversify partnerships as regional tensions and trade uncertainty persist.
